gaps.description: No paper validates polyp segmentation models in real clinical workflows or on actual edge hardware.

evidence.paperTitle: Attention-Guided Transformer Network for Polyp Segmentation
evidence.reason: No mention of deployment, latency, or hardware requirements despite being the most complex model

evidence.paperTitle: Efficient U-Net with Depthwise Separable Convolutions
evidence.reason: Achieves 120 FPS but tested only on standard GPU, not on clinical hardware or edge devices

evidence.paperTitle: Cross-Domain Polyp Segmentation via Style Transfer
evidence.reason: Adds computational overhead through style transfer but does not measure inference impact

gaps.reasoning: All three papers develop models intended for clinical use, yet none validate on actual clinical hardware or within a real clinical workflow. Paper-0 uses a heavy transformer without efficiency analysis. Paper-1, despite claiming edge suitability, tests only on a standard GPU. Paper-2 adds inference overhead without measuring it. This suggests a systematic gap between research validation and clinical deployment requirements.

gaps.description: No paper provides interpretability analysis or visualization of model decisions for clinical users.

evidence.paperTitle: Attention-Guided Transformer Network for Polyp Segmentation
evidence.reason: Uses attention mechanisms theoretically suited for interpretability but provides no attention visualization or saliency maps

evidence.paperTitle: Efficient U-Net with Depthwise Separable Convolutions
evidence.reason: No interpretability analysis despite model being intended for clinical decision support

gaps.reasoning: Both paper-0 and paper-1 propose models intended for clinical use but provide no mechanism for clinicians to understand or verify model predictions. Paper-0's attention mechanism could naturally support visualization but this is not explored. For clinical adoption, explainability is a prerequisite that none of the papers address.

gaps.description: Over-reliance on Kvasir-SEG limits the demonstrated generalizability of proposed methods.

evidence.paperTitle: Attention-Guided Transformer Network for Polyp Segmentation
evidence.reason: Uses Kvasir-SEG and CVC-ClinicDB — both are widely used but similar in distribution

evidence.paperTitle: Efficient U-Net with Depthwise Separable Convolutions
evidence.reason: Evaluates on Kvasir-SEG only — weakest generalizability evidence among the three

evidence.paperTitle: Cross-Domain Polyp Segmentation via Style Transfer
evidence.reason: Uses multiple datasets but all are from the same polyp segmentation domain

gaps.reasoning: Every paper relies on Kvasir-SEG, which has become a de facto benchmark. While paper-0 and paper-2 use additional datasets, all datasets are from the same narrow domain of polyp segmentation in colonoscopy. None of the papers validate on datasets from different anatomical sites or imaging modalities, limiting claims about generalizability to broader medical image segmentation tasks.

gaps.description: Inconsistent evaluation metrics across papers make direct comparison difficult.

evidence.paperTitle: Attention-Guided Transformer Network for Polyp Segmentation
evidence.reason: Reports only Dice score; no IoU, precision, recall, or clinical utility metrics

evidence.paperTitle: Cross-Domain Polyp Segmentation via Style Transfer
evidence.reason: Reports Dice improvement only; no absolute performance numbers or standard deviation

gaps.reasoning: The three papers report different sets of metrics: paper-0 reports only Dice, paper-1 reports Dice plus efficiency metrics, and paper-2 reports relative improvement. This inconsistency makes it difficult to directly compare methods. The field would benefit from a standardized evaluation protocol that includes both accuracy metrics and deployment-relevant measures.
